intro: Welcome! Real speakers often don't say exactly what they mean: 'It wasn't exactly a success' means it went badly, and 'Let me think about it' often means no. In this lesson you learn to hear attitudes and implied meaning, to follow messy, unplanned talk in interviews and panels, and to take lecture notes that keep what matters and skip the rest.
teachingNotes: Recap and build, in one line: from b1-listening-main-points the learner finds the main point and takes key-word notes (digits, → and +); from b2-listening-extended they follow signposts in long talks (Let me turn to…, The key point is…, To sum up), separate facts from opinions, know that the real opinion comes after however / that said (not after admittedly), and use ↑ ↓ → = ≠, e.g., approx., b/c, w/ and the idea of Cornell notes. Don't re-teach any of that. Today goes further: meaning that is NOT said directly, unplanned speech (interviews, panels), and deciding what is worth writing down in a lecture.

Implied meaning (makna tersirat) is taught as five patterns, each found in the WORDS, because the app's audio is one flat text-to-speech voice and its tone of voice is not reliable. (1) Understatement (mengecilkan): small or negative-of-positive words for a big problem: It wasn't exactly a success (= it failed), I've had better days (= a bad day), That could have gone better (= it went badly), a bit of a problem (= a big problem); also positive: British 'not bad' often = quite good. (2) Irony (ironi): positive words + a clearly bad situation = the opposite: Oh great, another meeting about meetings; Just what we needed; Perfect. The cue is the clash between the words and the facts. (3) Reluctance (keengganan): I suppose I could, if no one else is free; If I have to; It wouldn't be my first choice; Fine, I'll do it = yes, but unwillingly. (4) Hedged refusal (penolakan halus): That's an interesting idea, let me think about it; I'll see what I can do; Maybe next year = probably no. (5) Faint praise (pujian tipis): praising something small when asked about something important (asked about his reports: Well, he's always on time) = nothing good to say about the important thing. Tell learners that in real life tone helps too (a flat 'great', a long 'suuure'), but the words are always the safest evidence.

Unstructured speech (interviews, panel discussions): there's no neat plan, so teach the learner to track (a) who holds which view: panellists refer to each other by name (I'd push back on what Dimas said; I'm with Sari on that = I agree with Sari; I don't agree with Budi about the office), so note NAME = VIEW; (b) topic shifts with weak or no signposts (Anyway…, Oh, and…, Going back to…, Speaking of…); (c) self-corrections and false starts: the LAST version is the fact (We'll launch in May, well, June, realistically = June; about fifty, sorry, fifteen = 15; or rather, I mean, actually, let me rephrase that); (d) asides (selingan) that are not the main point (by the way, and they'll kill me for saying this, not that it matters, where was I?); (e) fillers to ignore (you know, I mean, sort of, kind of, well).

Lecture notes: listen for what the lecturer marks as important (The key point here is…, Let me stress…, This will come up again / you'll see this in the exam, Make a note of this, It's worth noting that…, If you remember one thing…) and mark it in the notes (!!, *, NB, 'exam'). New symbols on top of B2: ∴ = therefore / so (maka), ≈ = about, vs = compared with, NB = important. Cornell layout: a narrow left column for key words or questions, a wide right column for notes during the lecture, a 1–2 sentence summary at the bottom afterwards. Write numbers and names at once (digits; a name as you hear it, check the slides later); after a correction, cross out and keep the final version. Skip: examples you already know, repetition (In other words… = the same idea again), jokes, asides, fillers and the lecturer's own background stories.

Common errors to target: taking positive words literally (hearing 'Oh great' or 'perfect' as happy, 'interesting idea' as yes, 'he's always on time' as praise of his work); reading understatement as a small problem ('a few problems' when the company nearly failed); writing the first number or date instead of the corrected one; taking an aside or an example as the speaker's main point; mixing up who said what in a panel (reporting the view a speaker REJECTS as their own view); writing down everything, including examples you already know, and missing the point the lecturer stresses; missing a 'not' in 'it's not the price, it's the frequency'. Indonesian bridge: Indonesians already use soft refusals and understatement (nanti saya pikir-pikir dulu, lihat nanti ya, agak kurang), so link to that; the trap is assuming English speakers are always direct and taking their words at face value.

Limits: this is a skills lesson after B2, so listen texts use A0–B2 grammar only (past modals like could have gone better, conditionals, passive, reported speech are fine). No inversion, cleft sentences ('What I want to stress is…'), subjunctive or impersonal passives in the listen texts. Every `listen` is one speaker (a founder's interview answer, one panellist's turn, a lecture extract), at most 300 characters, and the prompt gives the context. Answers are short (an attitude word from a given list, the final corrected fact, a name, a note key word): accept the meaning, not exact words. At C1 some readings are subtle; only test cases where the words leave one clear interpretation. Contexts: an Indonesian startup founder on a podcast, a university lecture in Yogyakarta on urban transport, an online panel on remote work. Don't invent statistics about real organisations.

keyPoints.title: Hearing what people really mean
keyPoints.explanation: Speakers often say less, or the opposite, of what they mean. Five patterns: understatement (It wasn't exactly a success = it failed), irony (positive words + a bad situation: Oh great, another delay = annoyed), reluctance (I suppose I could, if no one else is free = yes, but unwillingly), hedged refusal (That's an interesting idea, let me think about it = probably no) and faint praise (asked about his work: Well, he's always on time = his work isn't good). Compare the words with the facts: when they don't match, the facts tell you the real meaning.

examples.en: Well, it wasn't exactly a success.
examples.id: Yah, itu bukan sukses juga sih. (maksudnya: gagal)

examples.en: Oh great, the system's down again. Just what I needed.
examples.id: Wah bagus, sistemnya mati lagi. Pas banget. (ironi: kesal)

examples.en: I suppose I could, if no one else is free.
examples.id: Ya, bisa sih, kalau tidak ada orang lain yang bisa. (enggan)

id.title: Menangkap maksud sebenarnya
id.explanation: Pembicara sering mengatakan lebih sedikit, atau kebalikan, dari maksudnya. Ada lima pola: understatement (mengecilkan: It wasn't exactly a success = gagal), ironi (kata positif + situasi buruk: Oh great, another delay = kesal), keengganan (I suppose I could, if no one else is free = mau, tapi terpaksa), penolakan halus (That's an interesting idea, let me think about it = kemungkinan besar tidak) dan pujian tipis (ditanya soal kerjanya: Well, he's always on time = kerjanya kurang bagus). Bandingkan kata-katanya dengan faktanya: kalau tidak cocok, faktanya yang memberitahumu maksud sebenarnya.

keyPoints.title: Following interviews and panels
keyPoints.explanation: Unplanned speech has no neat structure. Track four things: who holds which view (I'm with Sari on that = I agree with Sari; I'd push back on what Dimas said = I disagree with Dimas), topic changes with weak signposts (Anyway…, Oh, and…, Going back to…), self-corrections (May, well, June, realistically: the LAST version is the fact) and asides (by the way, not that it matters: not the main point). Ignore fillers like you know, I mean, sort of.

examples.en: We'll launch in May, well, June, realistically.
examples.id: Kami akan meluncur bulan Mei, eh, Juni, kalau realistis. (faktanya: Juni)
Saya sependapat dengan Sari soal itu.

examples.en: Anyway, where was I? Oh yes, the costs.
examples.id: Pokoknya, tadi sampai mana? Oh ya, biayanya. (kembali ke topik)

id.title: Mengikuti wawancara dan panel
id.explanation: Ucapan yang tidak direncanakan tidak punya struktur yang rapi. Ikuti empat hal: siapa berpendapat apa (I'm with Sari on that = saya setuju dengan Sari; I'd push back on what Dimas said = saya kurang setuju dengan Dimas), perpindahan topik dengan penanda yang lemah (Anyway…, Oh, and…, Going back to…), koreksi diri (May, well, June, realistically: versi TERAKHIR yang jadi faktanya) dan selingan (by the way, not that it matters: bukan poin utama). Abaikan kata pengisi seperti you know, I mean, sort of.

keyPoints.title: Lecture notes that keep what matters
keyPoints.explanation: Listen for what the lecturer marks as important: The key point here is…, Let me stress…, This will come up again, Make a note of this. Mark it in your notes (!!, NB, exam). Write numbers and names at once; after a correction, keep only the final version. Skip what you don't need: examples you already know, repetition, jokes, asides. Use symbols (↑ ↓ → ∴ ≈ vs) and abbreviations (e.g., b/c, w/), and a Cornell layout: key words on the left, notes on the right, a short summary at the bottom.

examples.en: Let me stress this, because it'll come up again.
examples.id: Saya tekankan ini, karena akan muncul lagi. (tandai: penting!)

examples.en: Fuel prices went up; therefore, more people took the bus.
examples.id: Harga BBM naik; karena itu, makin banyak orang naik bus. (Catatan: fuel ↑ ∴ bus users ↑)

id.title: Catatan kuliah yang menyimpan hal penting
id.explanation: Dengarkan apa yang ditandai dosen sebagai penting: The key point here is… (poin kuncinya…), Let me stress… (saya tekankan…), This will come up again (ini akan muncul lagi), Make a note of this (catat ini). Tandai di catatanmu (!!, NB, exam). Tulis angka dan nama saat itu juga; setelah ada koreksi, simpan versi terakhirnya saja. Lewati yang tidak perlu: contoh yang sudah kamu tahu, pengulangan, lelucon, selingan. Pakai simbol (↑ ↓ → ∴ ≈ vs) dan singkatan (e.g., b/c, w/), dan susunan Cornell: kata kunci di kiri, catatan di kanan, ringkasan pendek di bawah.

guidedPractice.prompt: After a meeting with a client in Jakarta, Budi says: 'Well, that could have gone better.' How did the meeting go: well or badly? Answer in one word.
guidedPractice.hint: This is understatement: a soft sentence for a bad result. If it had gone well, he would just say so.

guidedPractice.prompt: At the start of an online call, a colleague says: 'Oh great, another meeting about meetings.' Is she pleased or annoyed? Answer in one word.
guidedPractice.hint: Look for the clash: a positive word ('great') next to something nobody likes (a meeting about meetings). That's irony.

guidedPractice.prompt: A founder says on a podcast: 'We have about fifty, sorry, fifteen people in our Surabaya office.' How many people work in the Surabaya office? Write the number in digits.
guidedPractice.hint: After 'sorry', the speaker corrects the number. The last version is the fact.

guidedPractice.prompt: A lecturer in Yogyakarta says: 'Let me stress this: bus lanes only work if cars can't use them.' Which three words tell you that this point is important?
guidedPractice.hint: Find the words before the colon. They're a signal, not part of the content.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a short note (key words and symbols, not a sentence) for: 'Fuel prices went up; therefore, more people took the bus.'
expected: fuel prices ↑ ∴ more people take the bus
fuel prices up so more bus users
guidedPractice.hint: What went up? What was the result? Use ↑ for 'went up' and ∴ (or →) for 'therefore'.

independentPractice.prompt: In a panel discussion you hear: 'I'm with Rina on the cost, it's too high. But Pak Hasan's idea of a trial month? I can't see that working.' Whose idea does the speaker reject? Write the name.
independentPractice.hint: 'I'm with Rina' means 'I agree with Rina'. 'I can't see that working' is about someone else's idea.

independentPractice.prompt: You ask a colleague to help with your report. She answers: 'I'll see what I can do, but it's a really busy week.' Will she probably help? Answer yes or probably not.
independentPractice.hint: 'I'll see what I can do' + a reason why it's difficult is a polite way to prepare you for a no.

assessment.prompt: On an online panel about remote work, the host asks one panellist to lead a new working group. Listen to the answer. Which word best describes the panellist's attitude: enthusiastic, reluctant, proud or relieved? Write one word.
assessment.listen: Lead the working group? Well, I suppose I could, if no one else is free. I'm quite busy with the new project until March, so it wouldn't be my first choice. But if it really has to be someone from my team, then fine, I'll do it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: reluctant (I suppose I could, if no one else is free, it wouldn't be my first choice, fine, I'll do it = yes, but unwillingly). A synonym not from the list (unwilling, hesitant) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (enggan, terpaksa) = 60. 'enthusiastic' = 0 (the panellist agrees, but only if nobody else can). 'proud' / 'relieved' = 0 (nothing in the words shows them).

assessment.prompt: A startup founder from Jakarta talks on a podcast about the day the company's app was launched. Listen. Which word best describes how the founder felt about launch day: delighted, frustrated, relieved or bored? Write one word.
assessment.listen: Launch day? Oh, it was perfect. The server crashed at nine, the payment page didn't load for three hours, and our biggest investor tried the app live on TV at exactly that moment. Just what we needed.
assessment.rubric: Correct: frustrated ('perfect' and 'Just what we needed' are ironic: they sit next to a crash, a broken payment page and an embarrassing moment on TV). A synonym not from the list (annoyed, upset, angry, disappointed) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (kesal, frustrasi) = 60. 'delighted' = 0 (that's the literal meaning of 'perfect'; the facts show the opposite). 'relieved' / 'bored' = 0.

assessment.prompt: In an interview about her team, a manager, Bu Ani, is asked what she thinks of the reports written by a new team member, Fajar. Listen. Which word best describes her opinion of his reports: impressed, unimpressed, jealous or worried? Write one word.
assessment.listen: Fajar's reports? Well, he's always on time, I'll give him that. And they're very nicely formatted, with lovely colours. As for what's actually in them... let's just say he's always on time.
assessment.rubric: Correct: unimpressed (faint praise: asked about the reports, she only praises his punctuality and the colours, and avoids the content: 'let's just say he's always on time'). A similar answer not from the list (disappointed, negative, critical) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (tidak terkesan, kurang puas) = 60. 'impressed' = 0 (the praise is only for small things, not for the content). 'jealous' = 0. 'worried' = 30 (negative, but she doesn't express worry).

assessment.prompt: The founder of a Bandung startup is interviewed on a podcast about the company's story. Listen. In which year did the company really start? Write the year in digits.
assessment.listen: We started with three people in a kos in Bandung, back in 2019. No, sorry, 2018, the year I finished university. Then in 2020, well, everyone remembers 2020, we nearly closed. And now we're about forty people.
assessment.rubric: Correct: 2018 (the speaker corrects 2019 with 'No, sorry, 2018': the last version is the fact). 2019 = 0 (the version that was corrected). 2020 = 0 (the year they nearly closed). 40 / 3 = 0 (numbers of people, not a year).

assessment.prompt: This is one panellist's turn in an online panel discussion on remote work. Listen. Which person wants to close the office completely? Write the name.
assessment.listen: I agree with Sari that most people work better at home; the data's quite clear on that. But I don't agree with Budi about the office. He'd close it completely. I'd keep it, two days a week, mainly for new staff. Oh, and Rina asked about costs earlier. We'll come back to that.
assessment.rubric: Correct: Budi ('He'd close it completely' refers to Budi; the speaker disagrees with him). 'the speaker' / 'me' = 0 (the speaker would keep the office two days a week). 'Sari' = 0 (Sari's view is about working better at home). 'Rina' = 0 (Rina only asked about costs: an aside).

assessment.prompt: This is part of a lecture on urban transport at a university in Yogyakarta. Listen. You are taking Cornell notes. Write the ONE key word for the left (key words) column: the factor the lecturer says matters most.
assessment.listen: This is important, and you'll see it again in the exam. People don't choose the bus because it's cheap. They choose it because of frequency: how often it comes. If you have to wait forty minutes at a bus stop, you'll buy a motorbike. Simple as that.
assessment.rubric: Correct: frequency (how often the bus comes), marked as important by 'This is important, and you'll see it again in the exam'. 'price' / 'cheap' = 0 (the lecturer says people DON'T choose the bus because it's cheap). 'motorbike' = 20 (the result in the example, not the factor). '40 minutes' / 'waiting time' = 50 (a detail from the example that points to the right idea, but not the key word).

assessment.prompt: This is part of the same lecture on urban transport in Yogyakarta. Listen and take notes. About how many people an hour can a bus lane move? Write the number in digits.
assessment.listen: Let me give you the figures you'll need for your essay. A car lane moves about two thousand people an hour. A bus lane, if the buses run often, can move about six thousand, so one bus lane does the work of three car lanes. You don't need the other numbers on the slide.
assessment.rubric: Correct: 6000 (about six thousand people an hour). '6' = 70 if clearly meant as thousands (e.g. '6k'). 2000 = 0 (the car lane). 3 = 0 (one bus lane = three car lanes: a comparison, not the number of people).

material.title: Saying less, or the opposite, of what you mean

blocks.text:
At B2 you separated **facts** from the speaker's **opinion**, and you learnt that the real opinion comes after *however* or *that said*. Now the opinion is often **not said at all**: it's **implied** (tersirat). The speaker expects you to work it out. There are five common patterns:
- **Understatement** (mengecilkan): small, soft words for a big problem. *It wasn't exactly a success* = it failed. *I've had better days* = today was bad. *That could have gone better* = it went badly. *We had a bit of a problem* = a big problem.
- **Irony** (ironi): positive words for a bad situation, so they mean the opposite. *Oh great, another meeting about meetings.* *The train's late again. Perfect.* *Just what I needed.*
- **Reluctance** (keengganan): yes, but unwillingly. *I suppose I could, if no one else is free.* *If I have to.* *It wouldn't be my first choice.* *Fine, I'll do it.*
- **Hedged refusal** (penolakan halus): a polite way to say no. *That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it.* *I'll see what I can do.* *Maybe next year.*
- **Faint praise** (pujian tipis): when someone asks about something important, the speaker praises only something small. Asked about a colleague's work: *Well, he's always on time.* = there's nothing good to say about his work.

**The method:** compare the **words** with the **facts** around them. When they don't match (*perfect* + the server crashed), believe the facts.

id.text:
Di B2 kamu memisahkan **fakta** dari **opini** pembicara, dan kamu belajar bahwa opini sebenarnya datang setelah *however* atau *that said*. Sekarang opininya sering **tidak diucapkan sama sekali**: opininya **tersirat** (implied). Pembicara berharap kamu menangkapnya sendiri. Ada lima pola yang umum:
- **Understatement** (mengecilkan): kata-kata kecil dan halus untuk masalah besar. *It wasn't exactly a success* (bukan sukses juga sih) = gagal. *I've had better days* (aku pernah punya hari yang lebih baik) = hari ini buruk. *That could have gone better* (itu bisa berjalan lebih baik) = hasilnya buruk. *We had a bit of a problem* (kami ada sedikit masalah) = masalah besar.
- **Ironi**: kata positif untuk situasi buruk, jadi artinya kebalikannya. *Oh great, another meeting about meetings* (wah bagus, rapat lagi tentang rapat). *The train's late again. Perfect.* (Keretanya telat lagi. Sempurna.) *Just what I needed* (pas banget, ini yang aku butuhkan).
- **Keengganan** (reluctance): mau, tapi terpaksa. *I suppose I could, if no one else is free* (ya bisa sih, kalau tidak ada orang lain). *If I have to* (kalau memang harus). *It wouldn't be my first choice* (sebenarnya bukan pilihan utamaku). *Fine, I'll do it* (ya sudah, aku kerjakan).
- **Penolakan halus** (hedged refusal): cara sopan untuk bilang tidak. *That's an interesting idea. Let me think about it* (ide menarik, aku pikir-pikir dulu). *I'll see what I can do* (nanti aku lihat bisa atau tidak). *Maybe next year* (mungkin tahun depan).
- **Pujian tipis** (faint praise): ketika ditanya tentang hal yang penting, pembicara hanya memuji hal kecil. Ditanya tentang kerja seorang rekan: *Well, he's always on time* (yah, dia selalu tepat waktu) = tidak ada hal baik yang bisa dikatakan tentang kerjanya.

**Caranya:** bandingkan **kata-katanya** dengan **fakta** di sekitarnya. Kalau tidak cocok (*perfect* + servernya mati), percayai faktanya.

rows.en: Our first quarter wasn't exactly a success.
rows.id: Kuartal pertama kami bukan sukses juga sih.

rows.note: irony: positive word + bad fact = annoyed

id.note: ironi: kata positif + fakta buruk = kesal

rows.en: If I have to, I'll present it on Monday.
rows.id: Kalau memang harus, aku presentasikan hari Senin.

rows.en: I'll see what I can do, but it's a busy month.
rows.id: Nanti aku lihat bisa atau tidak, tapi bulan ini sibuk.

rows.en: Her presentation? Well, the slides were very colourful.
rows.note: faint praise: the content wasn't good
British understatement in a positive direction: often = quite good

id.note: understatement gaya Inggris ke arah positif: sering berarti cukup bagus

blocks.text: **You already know this from Indonesian.** *Nanti saya pikir-pikir dulu*, *lihat nanti ya* and *agak kurang* often mean no or bad, and *Bagus banget, macet lagi* is irony. The trap is to think English speakers always say exactly what they mean and to take their words at face value: *Oh great* = happy, *interesting idea* = yes, *he's always on time* = good worker. Understatement is especially common in **British** English (*not bad* = quite good; *a bit of a problem* = a serious problem); American speakers are often more direct, but they use irony and soft refusals too. In real life, tone of voice helps (a flat *great*, a long *suuure*), but the app's audio is one calm voice, so in this lesson the **words** are your evidence.

id.text: **Sebenarnya kamu sudah kenal ini dari bahasa Indonesia.** *Nanti saya pikir-pikir dulu*, *lihat nanti ya* dan *agak kurang* sering berarti tidak atau jelek, dan *Bagus banget, macet lagi* itu ironi. Jebakannya adalah mengira penutur bahasa Inggris selalu bicara apa adanya, lalu menelan kata-katanya mentah-mentah: *Oh great* = senang, *interesting idea* = setuju, *he's always on time* = pekerja yang bagus. Understatement sangat umum dalam bahasa Inggris **British** (*not bad* = cukup bagus; *a bit of a problem* = masalah serius); penutur Amerika sering lebih langsung, tapi mereka juga memakai ironi dan penolakan halus. Di dunia nyata, nada suara membantu (*great* yang datar, *suuure* yang panjang), tapi audio di aplikasi ini satu suara yang tenang, jadi di pelajaran ini **kata-katanya** adalah buktimu.

blocks.prompt: Your manager reads your proposal and says: 'Hmm. It's certainly very long.' What does she most probably think of it?
options: She thinks it's excellent and detailed.
She isn't happy with it, but she's saying so politely.
blocks.explain: This is faint praise: she's asked about the proposal and she comments only on its length, not on its ideas. If she liked it, she would praise the content. 'She hasn't read it' is wrong: she has just read it.

id.prompt: Manajermu membaca proposalmu lalu berkata: 'Hmm. It's certainly very long.' Kemungkinan besar apa pendapatnya?
id.explain: Ini pujian tipis: ia diminta pendapat tentang proposalnya, tapi hanya mengomentari panjangnya, bukan idenya. Kalau ia suka, ia akan memuji isinya. 'She hasn't read it' salah: ia baru saja membacanya.

id.title: Mengatakan lebih sedikit, atau kebalikan, dari maksudnya

material.title: Interviews and panels: messy, unplanned talk

blocks.text:
A lecture is planned; an interview or a panel discussion is not. People change topic, correct themselves, go off on a side story and come back. Signposts like *Firstly* or *Let me turn to* are rare. Track four things:
- **Who holds which view.** Panellists talk about each other: *I'm with Sari on that* (= I agree with Sari), *I'd push back a little on what Dimas said* (= I disagree a bit with Dimas), *Budi would close the office; I wouldn't*. In your head (or notes), keep a list: **NAME = VIEW**.
- **Topic shifts.** Often only a small word: *Anyway…*, *Oh, and…*, *Going back to…*, *Speaking of…*, or nothing at all.
- **Self-corrections and false starts.** Speakers change a number or a date as they talk: *We'll launch in May, well, June, realistically.* *About fifty, sorry, fifteen.* Words like *sorry*, *I mean*, *or rather*, *actually*, *well* before a new version tell you: **the last version is the fact**.
- **Asides** (selingan): small comments outside the main point: *by the way*, *and they'll kill me for saying this*, *not that it matters*, *where was I?* Enjoy them, but don't take them as the main point.

And ignore **fillers** (kata pengisi): *you know*, *I mean*, *sort of*, *kind of*, *like*. They give the speaker time to think; they don't carry meaning.

id.text:
Kuliah itu direncanakan; wawancara atau diskusi panel tidak. Orang berganti topik, mengoreksi dirinya sendiri, bercerita ke mana-mana lalu kembali. Penanda seperti *Firstly* atau *Let me turn to* jarang muncul. Ikuti empat hal:
- **Siapa berpendapat apa.** Para panelis saling membicarakan pendapat satu sama lain: *I'm with Sari on that* (= saya setuju dengan Sari), *I'd push back a little on what Dimas said* (= saya agak kurang setuju dengan Dimas), *Budi would close the office; I wouldn't* (Budi mau menutup kantornya; saya tidak). Di kepala (atau catatanmu), buat daftar: **NAMA = PENDAPAT**.
- **Perpindahan topik.** Sering hanya ditandai kata kecil: *Anyway…* (pokoknya / omong-omong), *Oh, and…* (oh, satu lagi), *Going back to…* (kembali ke…), *Speaking of…* (ngomong-ngomong soal…), atau tanpa penanda sama sekali.
- **Koreksi diri dan awal yang salah.** Pembicara mengganti angka atau tanggal sambil bicara: *We'll launch in May, well, June, realistically* (Mei, eh, Juni kalau realistis). *About fifty, sorry, fifteen* (sekitar lima puluh, maaf, lima belas). Kata seperti *sorry*, *I mean*, *or rather* (atau lebih tepatnya), *actually*, *well* sebelum versi baru memberitahumu: **versi terakhir itulah faktanya**.
- **Selingan** (aside): komentar kecil di luar poin utama: *by the way*, *and they'll kill me for saying this* (mereka bakal marah aku bilang begini), *not that it matters* (bukan berarti itu penting), *where was I?* (tadi sampai mana?). Nikmati saja, tapi jangan anggap itu poin utama.

Dan abaikan **kata pengisi** (filler): *you know*, *I mean*, *sort of*, *kind of*, *like*. Kata-kata itu memberi pembicara waktu berpikir; tidak membawa makna.

rows.en: There were about thirty, no, closer to forty people there.
rows.id: Ada sekitar tiga puluh, eh, hampir empat puluh orang di sana.

rows.en: The CEO, or rather the deputy CEO, will speak first.
rows.id: CEO-nya, atau lebih tepatnya wakil CEO-nya, akan bicara duluan.
rows.note: 'or rather' = the next version is the correct one

rows.en: I'd push back a little on what Dimas said.
rows.id: Saya agak kurang setuju dengan yang dikatakan Dimas.

rows.en: Sari's point about travel time is fair, though.
rows.id: Tapi poin Sari soal waktu perjalanan itu masuk akal.

rows.en: My team, and they'll kill me for saying this, loves Friday lunch more than the work.
rows.id: Timku, dan mereka bakal marah aku bilang begini, lebih suka makan siang hari Jumat daripada kerjanya.
rows.note: an aside: a joke, not the main point

rows.en: Anyway, going back to the costs…
rows.note: the speaker returns to the main topic

blocks.text: **Two traps.** First, the **first number you hear is not always the fact**: Indonesian learners often write it down at once and miss the correction a second later. Wait for the end of the sentence. Second, in a panel, people often **repeat someone else's view in order to reject it** (*He thinks new graduates learn best at home. In my experience, they don't*). The view you hear first may be the one the speaker disagrees with: check who it belongs to.

id.text: **Dua jebakan.** Pertama, **angka pertama yang kamu dengar belum tentu faktanya**: pelajar Indonesia sering langsung mencatatnya lalu ketinggalan koreksinya sedetik kemudian. Tunggu sampai kalimatnya selesai. Kedua, dalam panel, orang sering **mengulang pendapat orang lain untuk menolaknya** (*He thinks new graduates learn best at home. In my experience, they don't* = Dia pikir lulusan baru paling baik belajar di rumah. Menurut pengalaman saya, tidak). Pendapat yang pertama kamu dengar bisa jadi justru yang ditolak pembicara: cek itu pendapat siapa.

blocks.prompt: In an interview, the head of an NGO in Surabaya says: 'We trained two hundred teachers last year, I mean, two hundred and fifty, if you count the online course.' How many teachers did they train, including the online course?
blocks.explain: 'I mean' introduces the corrected, more complete number: 250, including the online course. 200 is the first version. 50 is only the difference, not a number the speaker gives.

id.prompt: Dalam sebuah wawancara, kepala sebuah LSM di Surabaya berkata: 'We trained two hundred teachers last year, I mean, two hundred and fifty, if you count the online course.' Berapa guru yang mereka latih, termasuk kursus online-nya?
id.explain: 'I mean' (maksud saya) memperkenalkan angka yang sudah dikoreksi dan lebih lengkap: 250, termasuk kursus online. 200 adalah versi pertama. 50 hanya selisihnya, bukan angka yang disebut pembicara.

id.title: Wawancara dan panel: ucapan yang tidak rapi dan tidak direncanakan

material.title: Lectures: what to write and what to skip

blocks.text:
In a 90-minute lecture you can't write everything, and you shouldn't. Good notes keep **what the lecturer says matters** and skip the rest.

**Listen for the 'this is important' signals.** Lecturers tell you, often more than once:
- *The key point here is…* / *If you remember one thing from today…*
- *Let me stress…* / *I want to stress that…*
- *This will come up again* / *You'll see this in the exam*
- *Make a note of this* / *Write this down*
- *It's worth noting that…*
When you hear one, mark the note: **!!**, a star, **NB** (= note well, penting) or simply *exam*.

**Write at once:** numbers (as digits), names, dates, new technical terms. If you're not sure how to spell a name, write it as you hear it and check the slides later. After a correction (*sixty, sorry, sixteen*), cross out and keep the final version.

**Skip:** examples you already know (*You all know Malioboro…*), repetition (*In other words…* = the same idea again), jokes and personal stories, asides, fillers, and things the lecturer says you don't need (*You don't need the other numbers on the slide*).

id.text:
Dalam kuliah 90 menit kamu tidak bisa mencatat semuanya, dan memang tidak perlu. Catatan yang baik menyimpan **apa yang menurut dosen penting** dan melewati sisanya.

**Dengarkan sinyal 'ini penting'.** Dosen memberitahumu, sering lebih dari sekali:
- *The key point here is…* (poin kuncinya di sini…) / *If you remember one thing from today…* (kalau kalian ingat satu hal saja hari ini…)
- *Let me stress…* / *I want to stress that…* (saya tekankan…)
- *This will come up again* (ini akan muncul lagi) / *You'll see this in the exam* (ini akan keluar di ujian)
- *Make a note of this* / *Write this down* (catat ini)
- *It's worth noting that…* (perlu dicatat bahwa…)
Kalau kamu mendengar salah satunya, tandai catatanmu: **!!**, tanda bintang, **NB** (= note well, penting) atau cukup tulis *exam*.

**Tulis saat itu juga:** angka (dalam digit), nama, tanggal, istilah teknis baru. Kalau tidak yakin ejaan sebuah nama, tulis sesuai yang kamu dengar lalu cek di slide nanti. Setelah ada koreksi (*sixty, sorry, sixteen*), coret dan simpan versi terakhirnya.

**Lewati:** contoh yang sudah kamu tahu (*You all know Malioboro…*), pengulangan (*In other words…* = ide yang sama lagi), lelucon dan cerita pribadi, selingan, kata pengisi, dan hal yang kata dosennya tidak perlu (*You don't need the other numbers on the slide* = kalian tidak perlu angka lain di slide).

rows.en: The key point here is that cheap parking brings more cars into the city centre.
rows.id: Poin kuncinya di sini adalah parkir yang murah membawa lebih banyak mobil ke pusat kota.

rows.en: This will come up again in week ten.
rows.id: Ini akan muncul lagi di minggu kesepuluh.
rows.note: mark it: you'll need it later

rows.en: I'm sure you've all been stuck in traffic on Jalan Kaliurang.
rows.id: Saya yakin kalian semua pernah terjebak macet di Jalan Kaliurang.

rows.en: In other words, cheap parking means more cars.
rows.id: Dengan kata lain, parkir murah berarti lebih banyak mobil.
rows.note: repetition: write it only if you missed the first version

id.note: pengulangan: catat hanya kalau kamu ketinggalan versi pertamanya

blocks.text: **A habit to change.** Many students in Indonesia learnt to copy what the lecturer writes on the board or the slides, and to write it neatly. In an English lecture, the slides are usually shared afterwards: the value of your notes is what the lecturer **says** that is not on the slides, especially the points they **stress**. Messy notes with the right key words beat neat notes of the wrong things.

id.text: **Kebiasaan yang perlu diubah.** Banyak pelajar di Indonesia terbiasa menyalin apa yang ditulis dosen di papan atau slide, dan menulisnya dengan rapi. Di kuliah berbahasa Inggris, slide biasanya dibagikan setelahnya: nilai catatanmu ada pada apa yang dosen **ucapkan** dan tidak ada di slide, terutama poin yang ia **tekankan**. Catatan berantakan dengan kata kunci yang tepat lebih berguna daripada catatan rapi tentang hal yang salah.

blocks.prompt: A lecturer says: 'You all know the story of how the Jakarta MRT was built, so I'll skip that. But make a note of this: most passengers walk less than one kilometre to the station.' What should you write in your notes?
options: The history of how the MRT was built
Most passengers walk < 1 km to the station !!
blocks.explain: 'Make a note of this' marks the important point: most passengers walk less than 1 km. The history is something the lecturer skips because you already know it. It isn't 'just an example': it's the point the lecturer tells you to write down.

id.prompt: Seorang dosen berkata: 'You all know the story of how the Jakarta MRT was built, so I'll skip that. But make a note of this: most passengers walk less than one kilometre to the station.' Apa yang sebaiknya kamu tulis di catatanmu?
id.explain: 'Make a note of this' (catat ini) menandai poin penting: kebanyakan penumpang berjalan kurang dari 1 km. Sejarahnya justru dilewati dosen karena kamu sudah tahu. Ini bukan 'sekadar contoh': ini poin yang dosen minta kamu catat.

id.title: Kuliah: apa yang dicatat dan apa yang dilewati

blocks.text:
At B2 you met the idea of **Cornell notes**. Here's how a page looks for a lecture on urban transport in Yogyakarta:
- **Left column (narrow), key words or questions:** *parking fees*, *why fewer car trips?*
- **Right column (wide), notes during the lecture:** *parking fees ↑ → car trips to centre ↓ !! exam*; *e.g. city centres w/ high fees*
- **Bottom, summary after the lecture (1–2 sentences):** *Higher parking fees make people leave the car at home and take the bus.*

The left column is for later: cover the right column and test yourself with the key words before an exam.

**Symbols and abbreviations.** From B2: **↑** goes up, **↓** goes down, **→** leads to, **=** is / means, **≠** is not, **e.g.** for example, **b/c** because, **w/** with, **w/o** without, **approx.** about. New today: **∴** therefore (maka / jadi), **≈** about, roughly, **vs** compared with, **NB** important. You can also make your own short forms (*govt*, *Yk* for Yogyakarta, *pax* for passengers): just use them the same way every time. Notes can mix English and Indonesian.

id.text:
Di B2 kamu sudah kenal ide **catatan Cornell**. Begini satu halamannya untuk kuliah tentang transportasi kota di Yogyakarta:
- **Kolom kiri (sempit), kata kunci atau pertanyaan:** *parking fees* (tarif parkir), *why fewer car trips?*
- **Kolom kanan (lebar), catatan selama kuliah:** *parking fees ↑ → car trips to centre ↓ !! exam*; *e.g. city centres w/ high fees*
- **Bagian bawah, ringkasan setelah kuliah (1–2 kalimat):** *Higher parking fees make people leave the car at home and take the bus.* (Tarif parkir yang lebih tinggi membuat orang meninggalkan mobil di rumah dan naik bus.)

Kolom kiri dipakai nanti: tutup kolom kanan dan uji dirimu dengan kata kuncinya sebelum ujian.

**Simbol dan singkatan.** Dari B2: **↑** naik, **↓** turun, **→** menyebabkan, **=** adalah / artinya, **≠** bukan, **e.g.** misalnya, **b/c** karena, **w/** dengan, **w/o** tanpa, **approx.** kira-kira. Baru hari ini: **∴** maka / jadi (therefore), **≈** kira-kira, **vs** dibandingkan dengan, **NB** penting. Kamu juga boleh membuat singkatanmu sendiri (*govt* untuk pemerintah, *Yk* untuk Yogyakarta, *pax* untuk penumpang): asal dipakai dengan cara yang sama setiap kali. Catatan boleh campur bahasa Inggris dan Indonesia.

rows.en: Car use has gone up, so air quality has got worse.
rows.id: Penggunaan mobil naik, jadi kualitas udara memburuk.

rows.en: A bus pass costs roughly a third of the cost of petrol.
rows.id: Kartu langganan bus harganya kira-kira sepertiga biaya bensin.

rows.en: Compared with Jakarta, Yogyakarta has far fewer trains.
rows.id: Dibandingkan Jakarta, Yogyakarta punya jauh lebih sedikit kereta.

blocks.prompt: Which note matches this sentence from a lecture? 'Ticket prices have doubled; therefore, fewer students are taking the train.'
blocks.explain: 'Doubled' = ×2, 'therefore' = ∴, and 'fewer students' = ↓. The second option reverses both changes. The third reverses cause and result: the price is the cause, not the effect.

id.prompt: Catatan mana yang cocok dengan kalimat dari kuliah ini? 'Ticket prices have doubled; therefore, fewer students are taking the train.'
id.explain: 'Doubled' (naik dua kali lipat) = ×2, 'therefore' (maka) = ∴, dan 'fewer students' (makin sedikit mahasiswa) = ↓. Pilihan kedua membalik kedua perubahannya. Pilihan ketiga membalik sebab dan akibat: harganya adalah sebab, bukan akibat.

resources.title: An interview about two books
resources.note: C1 listening: a radio presenter talks with a writer and a book critic about two novels on troubled families. Three voices, mild disagreement and opinions that are often implied rather than said: practise following who thinks what. With transcript and exercises.

id.note: Menyimak C1: seorang penyiar radio berbincang dengan seorang penulis dan seorang kritikus buku tentang dua novel tentang keluarga yang bermasalah. Tiga suara, sedikit perbedaan pendapat dan opini yang sering tersirat, bukan diucapkan langsung: latihan mengikuti siapa berpendapat apa. Ada transkrip dan latihannya.

resources.title: The history of hand gestures
resources.note: C1 listening: a lecture on the history of four gestures (the salute, the thumbs up, the high five and the handshake). Practise lecture notes: one key word per gesture on the left, the history on the right, and a summary at the end. With transcript and gap-fill exercises.

id.note: Menyimak C1: kuliah tentang sejarah empat gerakan tangan (hormat, jempol, tos dan jabat tangan). Latihan mencatat kuliah: satu kata kunci per gerakan di kiri, sejarahnya di kanan, dan ringkasan di akhir. Ada transkrip dan latihan isian.

id.intro: Selamat datang! Penutur asli sering tidak mengatakan persis apa yang mereka maksud: 'It wasn't exactly a success' berarti hasilnya buruk, dan 'Let me think about it' sering berarti tidak. Di pelajaran ini kamu belajar menangkap sikap dan makna tersirat, mengikuti obrolan yang tidak rapi di wawancara dan panel, dan membuat catatan kuliah yang menyimpan hal penting dan melewati sisanya.
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana aku tahu seseorang sedang berironi kalau aku tidak bisa mendengar nada suaranya?
Apakah 'not bad' itu pujian dalam bahasa Inggris British?
Apa saja yang sebaiknya kulewati saat mencatat kuliah?

assessment.lim-1: Dalam panel online tentang kerja jarak jauh, pembawa acara meminta seorang panelis memimpin kelompok kerja baru. Dengarkan jawabannya. Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan sikap panelis itu: enthusiastic, reluctant, proud atau relieved? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.lim-2: Seorang pendiri startup dari Jakarta bercerita di podcast tentang hari peluncuran aplikasi perusahaannya. Dengarkan. Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan perasaan si pendiri tentang hari peluncuran itu: delighted, frustrated, relieved atau bored? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.lim-3: Dalam wawancara tentang timnya, seorang manajer, Bu Ani, ditanya pendapatnya tentang laporan yang ditulis anggota tim baru, Fajar. Dengarkan. Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan pendapatnya tentang laporan Fajar: impressed, unimpressed, jealous atau worried? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.lim-4: Pendiri sebuah startup di Bandung diwawancarai di podcast tentang kisah perusahaannya. Dengarkan. Tahun berapa perusahaan itu sebenarnya mulai? Tulis tahunnya dengan digit.
assessment.lim-5: Ini giliran bicara seorang panelis dalam diskusi panel online tentang kerja jarak jauh. Dengarkan. Siapa yang ingin menutup kantornya sepenuhnya? Tulis namanya.
assessment.lim-6: Ini bagian dari kuliah tentang transportasi kota di sebuah universitas di Yogyakarta. Dengarkan. Kamu sedang membuat catatan Cornell. Tulis SATU kata kunci untuk kolom kiri (kata kunci): faktor yang menurut dosen paling penting. Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.lim-7: Ini bagian dari kuliah yang sama tentang transportasi kota di Yogyakarta. Dengarkan dan buat catatan. Kira-kira berapa orang per jam yang bisa diangkut satu jalur bus? Tulis angkanya dengan digit.
